title: Why Leaves Change Color
paragraphs: Every autumn, many trees put on a colorful show.
Their green leaves turn yellow, orange, red, and even purple.
Have you ever wondered where these beautiful colors come from?
The answer is hiding inside each leaf.
Leaves are green because they are full of chlorophyll.
Chlorophyll is a pigment, or natural coloring, that soaks up sunlight.
The tree uses this light to make sugar, which is its food.
All summer long, the tree keeps making new chlorophyll.
There is so much green that it covers up the other colors.
When autumn comes, the days get shorter and the nights get longer.
Trees can sense this difference, and they start to get ready for winter.
They stop making new chlorophyll, and the old chlorophyll slowly breaks down.
As the green fades, yellow and orange colors begin to appear.
These colors come from carotenoids, the same kind of pigment that makes carrots orange.
They were in the leaf the whole time, hidden under the green.
Red and purple colors work in a different way.
They come from pigments called anthocyanins, and most of them are made in autumn.
Sunny days and cool nights help trees make more of these red pigments.
That is one reason some autumns are more colorful than others.
Finally, a thin layer of cells grows where each leaf joins its branch.
The leaf is sealed off, and soon it drifts down to the ground.

title: The Kid Nobody Picked: Stephen Curry
paragraphs: Today, Stephen Curry is famous for his amazing three-point shots.
But when he was young, many people did not think he would become a superstar.
In high school, he was small and very thin.
He also shot the ball from down low, near his waist.
Taller players could easily block that shot.
So one summer, Curry worked hard to change his shot.
He learned to release the ball higher, from above his head.
It was difficult, and he later called it his most frustrating summer.
Still, he kept practicing until the new shot felt natural.
When it was time for college, the big schools did not want him.
Virginia Tech, his father's old college, said he could join the team without a scholarship.
Instead, Curry chose Davidson College, a small school with a coach who believed in him.
In 2008, he helped Davidson reach the last eight teams in the national tournament.
The next year, the Golden State Warriors picked him for the NBA.
Curry never stopped practicing.
In 2020, after one practice, he made 105 three-pointers in a row.
In the 2015-16 season, he made 402 three-pointers, which is still the record for one season.
In 2021, he passed Ray Allen for the most three-pointers in NBA history.
In 2025, he became the first player to make 4,000 of them.
He has also won four NBA championships with the Warriors.
The skinny kid that few teams wanted became one of the greatest shooters in history.

title: Japan's Bullet Trains and the Kingfisher
paragraphs: Japan has some of the fastest trains in the world.
They are called Shinkansen, but many people call them bullet trains.
The first line opened on October 1, 1964, just before the Tokyo Olympics.
It connected two big cities, Tokyo and Osaka.
Those first trains were built to travel at 210 kilometers per hour.
Today, bullet trains are even faster.
On one line, they zoom along at up to 320 kilometers per hour.
Yet speed is not the only thing that makes them special.
Since 1964, no passenger has died in a bullet train crash or derailment.
The trains are also famous for being on time.
On the line between Tokyo and Osaka, the average train is less than one minute late.
However, fast trains once had a noisy problem.
When a train rushed into a tunnel, it squeezed the air in front of it.
The air burst out of the far end with a loud boom.
This sound bothered the people who lived nearby.
An engineer named Eiji Nakatsu loved watching birds, and he thought of the kingfisher.
A kingfisher dives into water to catch fish.
Its long, pointed beak lets it enter the water with hardly any splash.
So Nakatsu's team gave a new train a long nose shaped like that beak.
This train, the 500 Series, was much quieter in tunnels.
It also went about 10 percent faster and used about 15 percent less electricity.
Sometimes the best ideas come from watching nature closely.

title: Owen's Volcano
paragraphs: Owen had one week to build a volcano for the science fair.
He wanted it to be the best one in his whole class.
On Saturday, he shaped a mountain of clay around a plastic cup.
Then he quickly dumped in baking soda and vinegar.
He stepped back and waited for a giant eruption.
Nothing exciting happened.
A few tiny bubbles crawled over the edge and stopped.
Owen stared at the sad little puddle for a long time.
Then he pushed the volcano away and stomped up to his room.
At dinner, he did not even touch his favorite chocolate pudding.
The next morning, his older sister Mia knocked on his door.
"Show me exactly what you did," she said.
Owen found the recipe and read it again, slowly this time.
It said to use three spoonfuls of baking soda, but he had used only one.
He had also guessed the amount of vinegar instead of using a measuring cup.
"I was rushing," Owen said quietly.
This time, Owen measured every ingredient with care.
He even counted five drops of red food coloring.
He checked the recipe twice before he poured anything.
Red foam bubbled up and spilled down the sides of the mountain.
Owen jumped up and cheered so loudly that the dog started barking.
On his science fair poster, he wrote a new rule in big letters: "Check first, then pour."

title: Why Is the Ocean Salty?
paragraphs: If you have ever gulped seawater at the beach, you know it tastes terrible.
On average, ocean water is about 3.5 percent salt.
That sounds small, but it makes seawater unsafe for people to drink.
Strangely, most rivers taste fresh, even though they pour into the sea.
So where does the ocean's salt come from?
Surprisingly, much of it begins on land, inside ordinary rocks.
When rain falls, it mixes with carbon dioxide gas in the air, which makes it slightly acidic.
Over many years, this weak acid breaks down rocks and dissolves bits of salts and minerals.
Streams and rivers then carry these minerals all the way to the ocean.
River water holds so little salt, though, that it still tastes fresh to us.
Salt also enters the ocean from deep below.
On the seafloor, seawater seeps into cracks in the Earth's crust, where hot magma heats it.
The hot water dissolves minerals from the rock and flows back out through hydrothermal vents.
Once salt reaches the ocean, it usually stays there.
The sun's heat makes water evaporate, but the salt cannot rise with it, so it stays behind.
Sea creatures use up some elements, but sodium and chloride, the parts of table salt, keep building up.
Some lakes are even saltier than the ocean.
The Dead Sea, a lake in the Middle East, has rivers flowing in but none flowing out.
In the hot desert, its water can only escape by evaporating, so the salt keeps piling up.
As a result, the Dead Sea is more than five times saltier than the ocean.
Its water is so heavy with salt that visitors float easily, like corks!

title: Emperor Penguins: Winter Champions
paragraphs: Antarctica in winter may be the harshest place on Earth for an animal to raise a family.
Temperatures can drop below minus 50 degrees Celsius.
Icy winds can blow faster than 150 kilometers per hour.
Most birds would leave, yet emperor penguins choose this exact season to have their chicks.
In autumn, each female lays a single egg.
She passes it carefully to her partner and walks back to the sea to feed.
The male balances the egg on top of his feet.
He covers it with a warm fold of skin called a brood pouch.
Inside the pouch, the egg stays at about 38 degrees Celsius.
For more than two months, the father patiently guards the egg without eating any food at all.
To survive the dangerous storms, crowds of fathers squeeze together in a tight group called a huddle.
Deep inside a huddle, it can get as warm as about 37 degrees Celsius, close to a human's body temperature.
By the time the egg hatches, the father has gone about four months without a meal.
He may lose nearly half of his body weight.
Around July, the mother returns with food in her stomach for the new chick.
Then the tired father can finally waddle off to the sea to eat.
Emperor penguins are also incredible underwater.
They can dive more than 500 meters below the surface to hunt for food.
On a long hunting dive, an emperor penguin can hold its breath for about 20 minutes.
Their bodies are built for both the deep sea and the frozen ice.
With teamwork and patience, these tough birds raise chicks in one of Earth's coldest places.

title: Marie Curie and Her Two Elements
paragraphs: Marie Curie was born Maria Sklodowska in Warsaw, Poland, in 1867.
As a girl, she loved science, but women in Warsaw could not attend a regular university.
So at age 24, she moved to Paris to study physics and mathematics at the Sorbonne.
She had very little money, but she worked hard and earned a physics degree in 1893.
In Paris, she met a scientist named Pierre Curie, and they married in 1895.
Marie became curious about invisible rays that came out of certain rocks.
A dark rock called pitchblende gave off much stronger rays than she expected.
She guessed that unknown elements must be hiding inside it.
After months of hard work with Pierre, in 1898 she found two new elements.
Marie named the first one polonium, after her home country of Poland.
They called the second one radium, from a Latin word meaning ray.
Marie even created a new word for this strange power: radioactivity.
In 1903, Marie and Pierre shared the Nobel Prize in Physics with another scientist, Henri Becquerel.
This made Marie the first woman ever to win a Nobel Prize.
Sadly, Pierre died in a street accident in 1906, but Marie kept working.
In 1911, she won a second Nobel Prize, this time in Chemistry.
She is still the only person to win Nobel Prizes in two different sciences.
Today, both of her elements have their own boxes on the periodic table.
Polonium is element number 84, and radium is element number 88.
Their symbols are Po and Ra, and Po is a little reminder of Poland.
Next time you see the periodic table, find box 84 and remember the girl from Warsaw who followed her curiosity.

title: Look, Think, Move, Check
paragraphs: Jiho loved chess, but he loved playing fast even more.
At his first tournament, he sat across from a quiet girl named Clara.
Whenever Clara moved, Jiho immediately grabbed a piece and slammed it down on a new square.
He wanted to look like a champion who never needed to think.
On his tenth move, he pushed his knight forward without checking the board.
Clara's bishop slid across the board and captured it in one smooth move.
Jiho stared at the empty square, and his ears felt hot.
He tried to win the knight back by hurrying, but he made two more mistakes.
Clara won the game in less than twenty minutes.
She shook his hand politely, but Jiho could barely look at her.
During the break, Coach Han handed him a cup of water and a small white card.
On the card were four words: Look, Think, Move, Check.
Coach Han explained that he should first look at what his opponent had just done.
Next, he should think about which of his pieces could be attacked.
Only then should he move, and afterward, he should check the board again for danger.
"Fast hands make slow games," Coach Han said with a smile.
In the second game, Jiho sat on his hands whenever he felt the urge to rush.
Before each move, he quietly whispered the four words to himself.
Once, he almost moved his queen into a dangerous trap, but the word "check" stopped him just in time.
The game continued for almost an hour, and it finally ended in a draw.
Jiho went home without a trophy, but the little card stayed in his pocket for every game after that.

title: The Race to the Bottom of the World
paragraphs: In 1911, two teams set out across Antarctica, each hoping to be the first to reach the South Pole.
One team was led by Roald Amundsen, a calm and careful explorer from Norway.
The other was led by Robert Falcon Scott, a British navy officer who had explored Antarctica before.
Both leaders knew that the frozen continent could turn deadly in the blink of an eye.
Amundsen was convinced that dogs and skis were the fastest way to travel across the ice.
He set off on October 19, 1911, with four other men, four sleds, and 52 dogs.
Months earlier, his team had stored food in depots along the route, so they would not run short on the way back.
Scott chose a mix of ponies, motor sleds, and dogs.
Unfortunately, the machines soon broke down, and the ponies grew too weak to go on.
In the end, Scott's men had to drag their heavy sleds through the snow by themselves.
On December 14, 1911, Amundsen and his four teammates reached the South Pole and raised the Norwegian flag.
Before heading home, they left a tent with a letter for the king of Norway and a note asking Scott to deliver it.
About five weeks later, on January 17, 1912, Scott's exhausted party of five finally arrived.
Instead of a victory, they found the Norwegian tent already waiting for them.
The long walk back turned into a disaster.
Storms, hunger, and bitter cold wore the men down, and none of the five made it home alive.
Scott and his last two companions died in their tent, only about eleven miles from a store of food and fuel.
Amundsen's team, on the other hand, made it back safely without losing a single man.
Today, people still look back on this race as a lesson in how careful planning can mean the difference between life and death.

title: The Man Who Played Cards with the Elements
paragraphs: By 1869, scientists had found 63 elements, but nobody could figure out how they fit together.
It was like a box of puzzle pieces with no picture on the lid.
A Russian chemistry professor named Dmitri Mendeleev was writing a textbook, and he wanted to put the elements in order.
People like to tell a story about how he finally cracked the puzzle.
In the story, he wrote each element's name and weight on its own card, with notes about how it behaved.
Then he laid the cards out in rows and shuffled them around for hours, the way someone plays solitaire.
When he lined them up by atomic weight, a big surprise jumped out at him.
Elements that behaved alike kept popping up at regular intervals, like a pattern repeating on wallpaper.
In 1869, he shared his new table with other chemists in Russia.
The boldest part was not what he put into it, but what he left out.
Wherever the pattern skipped a step, he left an empty space and insisted that a missing element belonged there.
He even predicted what each missing element would be like and gave it a name, such as eka-aluminium or eka-silicon.
Some chemists doubted him, but soon the empty boxes began to fill in.
In 1875, a French chemist discovered gallium, a shiny metal that can melt in your hand.
It matched eka-aluminium closely, but the chemist found it lighter for its size than Mendeleev had predicted.
Mendeleev wrote to him and suggested that he measure it again.
Sure enough, the new result came out almost exactly as Mendeleev had said.
Then, in 1886, germanium turned up and matched eka-silicon just as well.
Today, the periodic table holds 118 elements, and number 101 is named mendelevium in his honor.
Not bad for a man who started out with a pile of cards and a hunch.

title: Venice: The City That Stands on a Forest
paragraphs: Imagine stepping out your front door and climbing straight into a boat instead of a car.
In Venice, a beautiful city in northern Italy, that is everyday life for many people.
The city is spread across 118 small islands in a shallow lagoon, and canals replace roads.
More than 400 bridges link the islands together, so you can also get around on foot.
Venice is not actually floating, even though it might look that way.
Centuries ago, builders drove millions of wooden poles, called piles, deep into the muddy bottom of the lagoon.
They kept pounding until the poles reached a layer of hard clay.
On top of these foundations, they laid planks and stone, then built houses, churches, and palaces.
Since there is almost no oxygen in the mud, the tiny living things that usually rot wood cannot survive there.
Getting around Venice takes some getting used to.
Residents hop on a vaporetto, a water bus that stops at floating platforms along the canals.
Visitors often ride in a gondola, a long black boat moved by a rower with a single oar.
Even ambulances, fire engines, and garbage trucks are replaced by boats here.
Living on the water has a serious downside, though.
Dozens of times every year, powerful winds and high tides push seawater into the streets.
Venetians call this kind of flooding acqua alta, which means high water in Italian.
In November 2019, the water rose so high that Saint Mark's Square ended up under about a meter of water.
To fight back, Italy built MOSE, a system of 78 enormous gates that rest on the seabed at the three entrances to the lagoon.
When a dangerous tide is coming, air is pumped into the gates so that they rise up and hold back the sea.
In October 2020, the gates were raised against a storm for the first time, and the city stayed dry.

title: The Case of the Fox Notes
paragraphs: For three weeks, someone had been slipping mysterious notes into Theo's backpack.
Each note was written in purple ink and signed with nothing but a tiny drawing of a fox.
One said "Your rocket drawing was awesome," and another wished him luck on his difficult spelling test.
Theo loved receiving them, but not knowing who had sent them was driving him up the wall.
So he decided to crack the case like a real detective, carefully writing down every clue in a notebook.
First, he noticed that the notes only showed up on Tuesdays and Thursdays, right after art class.
His best friend, Ravi, was in a different class and never had art with Theo, so the timing did not fit.
Besides, Ravi wrote in big, messy capital letters, while the fox used neat, beautiful, curly handwriting.
The third note was the most curious one of all.
It said, "I hope Biscuit is feeling better," and Biscuit was his grandmother's elderly cat.
Theo had mentioned the sick cat only once, in a whisper, to the two kids at his art table, Jonah and Mia.
Their art teacher was across the room cleaning up a terrible paint spill, so she could not possibly have overheard.
That left only two possible suspects, so Theo flipped back through his notebook to compare the dates.
The Biscuit note had arrived on a Thursday, during the very week that Jonah stayed home with the flu.
Jonah had not set foot in school for a single day that week.
With his investigation finished, Theo grinned and tore a fresh page out of his notebook.
The next Tuesday, after art, he tucked a note of his own into the backpack of the one person who fit every clue.
Instead of a fox, he signed it with a tiny magnifying glass.
It said, "Thanks for the notes, Fox, and would you like to sit together at lunch?"

title: How Basketball Was Born
paragraphs: In 1891, a teacher named James Naismith had a problem.
He worked at a school in Springfield, Massachusetts.
Winter was cold and snowy, so his students could not play sports outside.
They were stuck in the gym, and they were getting bored and restless.
Naismith's boss gave him two weeks to invent a new indoor game.
He wanted a game that was active but not too rough.
He decided that players could not run while holding the ball.
This rule made players pass the ball to each other instead of crashing into each other.
Next, Naismith needed a goal.
He nailed two peach baskets to the railing of a balcony, about ten feet above the floor.
Because the goal was high up, players had to toss the ball gently instead of throwing it hard.
The baskets still had bottoms, so someone had to climb up and get the ball after every score!
Naismith wrote thirteen rules for his new game, and his students loved it.
Soon, people in other cities and countries started playing too.
Today, millions of people around the world play basketball, and the hoop is still ten feet high.

title: Why Do Balloons Float?
paragraphs: Have you ever let go of a balloon at a party and watched it fly up to the ceiling?
That balloon was probably filled with a gas called helium.
A balloon you blow up with your mouth does not float like that.
So what makes a helium balloon different?
Everything around us is made of tiny pieces called atoms.
The air around us is mostly made of nitrogen and oxygen.
Helium atoms are much lighter than the nitrogen and oxygen in the air.
Because helium is lighter than air, the air pushes the balloon up, just like water pushes a beach ball up in a pool.
Hydrogen is even lighter than helium, and it is number 1 on the periodic table.
Long ago, people filled giant airships with hydrogen.
But hydrogen catches fire very easily, and in 1937 a famous airship called the Hindenburg burst into flames.

An octopus has no bones, so it can squeeze its soft body through very small holes.
An octopus also has three hearts.
Two hearts pump blood to its gills, where it gets oxygen from the water.
The third heart pumps blood to the rest of its body.
Its blood is not red like ours; it is blue.
When a hungry shark comes near, an octopus has many tricks.
It can change the color of its skin in less than a second to match the rocks around it.
If the shark still finds it, the octopus squirts a cloud of dark ink and swims away.

Octopuses are also very smart.

title: The Second Free Throw
paragraphs: Leo stood at the free-throw line, and his hands were sweaty.
It was the last minute of the game, and his team was losing by one point.
If he made both shots, the Tigers would win.
Everyone in the gym was watching him.
Leo took a quick breath and threw the ball as fast as he could.
It hit the front of the rim and bounced away.
His face turned red, and he looked down at his shoes.
He wanted to run off the court and hide.
Then he remembered what Coach Kim always said: "Slow down. See the hoop, then shoot."
Leo bounced the ball three times, just like he did at practice.
He bent his knees, looked at the front of the rim, and took his time.
Swish! The ball dropped through the net, and the game was tied.
The Tigers did not win that night; they lost in overtime.
But on the bus ride home, Leo was smiling.
He had learned that the shot he took slowly was the one that went in.

title: Why Do We Have Day and Night?
paragraphs: Every morning, the sun seems to climb up into the sky.
Every evening, it seems to sink down and disappear.
Long ago, many people believed that the sun traveled around Earth.
They were wrong, but it is easy to see why they thought so.
The truth is that Earth is the one that moves.
Our planet spins like a giant top, and it never stops.
It turns all the way around once about every 24 hours.
That is why one day and one night together last about 24 hours.
Earth spins from west to east, so the sun appears to rise in the east.
At night, the sun has not gone anywhere at all.
Scientists call this spinning rotation.
Only one half of Earth can face the sun at a time.
That half has daytime, with plenty of bright light.
The other half faces away from the sun, toward dark space.
That half has nighttime, and people there can see the moon and stars.
As Earth keeps turning, each place slowly moves from light into darkness.
So two friends far apart can have totally different times of day.
When it is lunchtime in Seoul, Korea, it is late at night in New York.
A child in Seoul might be eating lunch while a child in New York is sound asleep.
About twelve hours later, the two kids switch places.
Earth spins so fast that the middle of our planet moves over 1,500 kilometers per hour.
Yet we do not feel it, because we are all spinning together!

title: The Boy Who Was Too Small
paragraphs: Lionel Messi is one of the greatest soccer players who ever lived.
But as a boy, many people thought he was too small.
Leo was born in Rosario, Argentina, in 1987.
At age six, he joined a local youth club called Newell's Old Boys.
He could dribble past bigger kids as if they were standing still.
Around age ten, doctors found out why Leo was not growing much.
His body did not make enough growth hormone, a chemical that helps children grow.
To fix this, Leo needed a shot of medicine every night.
He bravely learned to give the shots to himself, right in his legs.
The medicine was expensive, and his family could not keep paying for it.
Then a famous club in Spain, FC Barcelona, heard about him.
In September 2000, thirteen-year-old Leo traveled there for a tryout.
The coaches loved him, but the club was slow to make a deal.
On December 14, 2000, a Barcelona leader named Carles Rexach finally acted.
He had no contract with him, so a waiter handed him a paper napkin.
He wrote a promise on it, and the deal was done.
Barcelona agreed to pay for Leo's medicine, and his family moved to Spain.
The tiny boy grew up to be about 170 centimeters tall.
In 2022, he led Argentina to win the World Cup.
In 2024, that famous napkin was sold for almost one million dollars!

title: Sea Otters: Sleepy Swimmers
paragraphs: Imagine falling asleep while floating on your back in the cold ocean.
That is exactly how sea otters take their naps.
These furry animals live along the rocky coasts of the Pacific Ocean.
They spend most of their lives in the water, and they are excellent swimmers.
Sleeping in the ocean has one big problem.
Waves and wind could carry a sleeping otter far away!
To stay in place, otters sometimes wrap themselves in long seaweed called kelp.
Kelp is attached to the sea floor, so it works like an anchor.
Otters also rest together in groups called rafts.
A raft often has about 50 otters.
Sometimes two otters even hold paws while they float.
Sea otters have no blubber, the thick layer of fat that keeps whales warm.
Instead, they have the thickest fur of any mammal on Earth.
One square inch of their skin can have up to one million hairs!
That is more hairs than most people have on their whole head.
To keep their fur clean and fluffy, otters spend a lot of time grooming.
Sea otters are also clever and creative tool users.
An otter dives down and grabs a clam along with a flat rock.
Back at the surface, it floats on its back and sets the rock on its chest.
Then it bangs the clam against the rock until the shell cracks open.
It can even keep a favorite rock in a pocket of loose skin under its arm.

title: The Sea Women of Jeju
paragraphs: On Jeju Island in Korea, some grandmothers have a very unusual job.
Almost every day, they pull on wetsuits and jump into the cold sea.
These women are called haenyeo, which means "sea women" in Korean.
People on Jeju have been diving for food for more than a thousand years.
Haenyeo do not carry oxygen tanks on their backs.
Instead, they take one deep breath and hold it.
Each dive lasts about one minute, and they can swim down about 10 meters.
That is about as deep as a three-story building is tall!
When they come back up, they let out their breath with a special whistling sound.
This sound is called sumbisori.
Underwater, haenyeo gather abalone, sea urchins, and other shellfish.
Some of them work in the sea for up to seven hours a day.
The divers are put into groups based on their skill.
The most experienced divers guide the younger ones.
They also help take care of the sea so that sea life can grow back.
Amazingly, some haenyeo are still diving in their 80s!
In 2016, UNESCO added their culture to a special list of important world treasures.
In 1970, Jeju had more than 14,000 haenyeo.
Today, there are fewer than 3,000, and most of them are over 70.
That is why many people hope that young divers will keep this amazing tradition alive.

title: The First Coins: Money from Lydia
paragraphs: Long ago, there were no coins or paper money anywhere in the world.
If people wanted something, they had to trade for it.
This kind of trading is called bartering.
A farmer might trade a basket of grain for a pair of sandals.
But bartering often caused big problems.
Imagine you have a cow, but you only want one loaf of bread.
You cannot cut your cow into tiny pieces to pay the baker!
Also, the baker might not even want a cow.
People needed something small and valuable that everyone would accept.
More than 2,600 years ago, a kingdom called Lydia found an answer.
Lydia was in the land that is now the country of Turkey.
The Lydians made some of the earliest coins in the world.
They used electrum, a natural mix of gold and silver.
Each small lump of metal was stamped with a picture, such as a lion's head.
The lion was a royal symbol, so it showed that the king stood behind the coin.
Coins made buying and selling much easier.
They were small, so people could carry them in a pouch.
They did not rot like grain or wander away like a cow.
Before coins, people often had to weigh pieces of metal each time they paid.
With the king's stamp, people could trust a coin without weighing it.
Soon, the idea of coins spread to Greece and many other places.
Every coin in your piggy bank comes from that clever idea.

title: The Line That Changed Basketball
paragraphs: Today, the three-pointer is one of basketball's most exciting plays.
But for a long time, every basket from the floor was worth just two points.
It did not matter how far away a player shot from.
Then one simple line on the court changed the game.
The ABA, another professional league, started using a three-point line in 1967.
Fans loved watching players launch long shots.
In 1979, the NBA decided to try the line too.
It was added for the 1979-80 season as a one-year test.
On October 12, 1979, Chris Ford of the Boston Celtics made the first three-pointer in NBA history.
In the NBA, the line is 23 feet 9 inches from the basket at the top of the arc.
In the corners, it is closer, only 22 feet away.
That is why many shooters love the corner three.
For three seasons in the 1990s, the NBA moved the whole line in to 22 feet.
Then it moved the line back out in 1997.
At first, teams did not shoot many threes.
In that first season, they tried fewer than three per game.
Many experts say Stephen Curry helped change that.
Around 2015, he and the Golden State Warriors won by making deep threes.
Other teams saw how well it worked and started shooting more threes too.
In the 2024-25 season, NBA teams took about 37 three-pointers in every game.
A shot that was once rare is now a giant part of basketball.

title: Theo's Lemonade Plan
paragraphs: On a hot Saturday morning, Theo had a brilliant idea.
He would open a lemonade stand in front of his house.
He squeezed a pile of lemons and stirred in sugar.
He even painted a sign that said "Cold Lemonade, 50 Cents!"
Theo was so excited that he did not stop to make a plan.
By ten o'clock, a line of thirsty neighbors stretched down the sidewalk.
Theo poured cup after cup as fast as he could.
Then he reached into the bag and felt nothing at all.
He had brought only twelve cups, and they were all gone!
Mr. Park from next door held out his hand.
"Um, do you have your own cup?" Theo asked with a nervous smile.
Mr. Park laughed and went home to get a coffee mug.
But the other customers walked away to buy drinks at the corner store.
Theo sat on the curb and frowned at his full jug of lemonade.
His mom sat beside him and asked, "What did you learn today?"
Theo thought for a long moment.
"A good idea also needs a good plan," he finally said.
That night, Theo wrote a list in his notebook.
He wrote down cups, ice, napkins, and a box for coins.
Next to each item, he guessed how many he would need.
Next to cups, he wrote "40" and underlined it twice.
The next Saturday, his stand stayed open all morning long.
He sold 36 cups and still had four left over.
Theo grinned, because his mistake had taught him how to plan.

title: Fluoride Shields for Your Teeth
paragraphs: What is the hardest part of your body?
Many people guess bone, but the answer is in your mouth.
It is tooth enamel, the shiny white outer layer of each tooth.
Enamel is the hardest material in the whole human body, even harder than your bones.
It works like a suit of armor, protecting the softer parts inside each tooth.
Still, enamel has a sneaky enemy.
Tiny germs called bacteria live in your mouth.
When you eat candy or other sugary food, these germs eat the sugar too.
Then they make acid, which slowly pulls minerals out of your enamel.
Over time, this can leave a small hole called a cavity.
That is why most toothpaste contains a helpful mineral called fluoride.
Fluoride comes from fluorine, which is element number 9 on the periodic table.
Fluoride helps put minerals back into weak spots in the enamel.
This makes teeth stronger and better at fighting acid.
It also makes it harder for the germs to make acid.
However, using more toothpaste is not better.
Kids who are three or older need only a pea-sized amount.
Children under three need even less, about the size of a grain of rice.
Always spit out the toothpaste instead of swallowing it.
A grown-up should watch younger kids brush to make sure they do it right.
Brush twice a day, and your enamel shield will stay strong.

title: Isaac Newton and the Pull of Gravity
paragraphs: Have you ever wondered why a dropped ball falls down instead of floating away?
About 360 years ago, a young English scientist named Isaac Newton wondered the same thing.
In 1666, a terrible disease called the plague closed his university, so he returned to his family's farm.
There, he had plenty of time to imagine and experiment.
Many people believe an apple fell on Newton's head and knocked the idea into him.
That part is only a myth.
Late in his life, Newton told his friend William Stukeley what had really happened.
He had been resting in a garden when he noticed an apple drop from a tree.
He began to wonder why apples always fell straight down, never sideways or upward.
Stukeley wrote the story down, which is how we know it today.
Newton decided that an invisible pull, which we now call gravity, draws everything toward Earth's center.
Then he had an even bigger idea.
Perhaps the same force that tugs on an apple also reaches all the way out to the Moon.
The Moon is traveling sideways very fast, so instead of crashing down, it keeps curving around Earth.
In 1687, Newton explained his ideas in a famous book called the Principia.
Gravity also hides a surprising secret.
Without air in the way, a heavy object and a light object fall at exactly the same rate.
On Earth, air pushes against a feather and slows it, but it barely affects a heavy hammer.
In 1971, astronaut David Scott tested this idea on the Moon, which has almost no air.
He released a hammer and a falcon feather at the same moment, and they landed together!

title: The Puffling Patrol of Iceland
paragraphs: Atlantic puffins are chunky seabirds with orange feet and colorful, striped beaks.
Some people call them the clowns of the sea.
Every spring, over a million puffins arrive at the Westman Islands, near the southern coast of Iceland.
They gather in one of the largest puffin colonies on the planet.
Each puffin family usually has just one egg, hidden in a burrow on a grassy cliff.
After the chick hatches, both parents deliver fish in their beaks.
A baby puffin is called a puffling, an adorable name for an adorable bird.
At about six weeks old, the puffling is ready to leave home.
In late August and September, it waits until dark and flutters toward the ocean.
Some pufflings, however, have difficulty on their very first flight.
Many experts believe the young birds follow moonlight to locate the sea.
On Heimaey, the only island where people live, the bright lights of the town confuse them.
Instead of reaching the waves, the lost birds tumble onto streets and parking lots.
Their new wings are too weak to lift them off flat ground, so cars and hungry animals become a danger.
That is when the Puffling Patrol springs into action.
For a few weeks every year, children grab flashlights and cardboard boxes and search the town at night.
They peek under parked cars and behind trash bins, gently scooping up every puffling they discover.
Volunteers carefully weigh the rescued birds, and the next day the kids carry them to the cliffs.
Then they toss the pufflings into the air, and the birds glide down to the ocean.
One pair of sisters once rescued 125 pufflings in a single season!

title: Roads and Knots of the Inca Empire
paragraphs: About 500 years ago, the Inca Empire stretched along the Andes Mountains of South America.
Its rulers had to govern millions of people.
They lived in deserts, jungles, and snowy mountain villages.
To hold this enormous empire together, the Incas built an astonishing network of roads.
Altogether, the Inca roads ran for about 40,000 kilometers.
That is almost enough to wrap around Earth once!
Two main highways ran from north to south, one near the coast and one high in the mountains.
Workers carved stone steps into steep slopes.
They also wove bridges out of grass to cross deep canyons.
One famous rope bridge stretched about 45 meters across a river, and villagers rebuilt it about every two years.
Rest stops called tambos, usually placed about a day's walk apart, gave travelers food and shelter.
The roads also carried important news, thanks to relay runners called chasquis.
Their stations often stood about 2.5 kilometers apart, so each runner sprinted only a short distance.
As he came close, he blew a seashell trumpet to warn the next runner to get ready.
Then he passed along his message, and the fresh runner dashed away.
Working together, the chasquis could deliver a message up to 300 kilometers in a single day.
Surprisingly, the Incas never used an alphabet.
Instead, they kept records on a quipu, a bundle of colorful strings tied with knots.
The type and position of each knot stood for a number, using a system based on tens, just like ours.
With quipus, officials could keep track of people, llamas, crops, and taxes.
Specially trained experts read the knots, and chasquis often carried quipus with spoken messages.

title: Mina Keeps Her Cool
paragraphs: Mina was the shortest player on the Hawks, but also the quickest and most determined.
Midway through the championship game, she lunged for a steal and accidentally slapped an opponent's arm.
The referee blew his whistle and pointed straight at her.
Mina's cheeks burned, and she stomped her foot so hard that everybody heard it.
Before she could argue, Coach Rivera called a timeout and waved her over to the bench.
"I barely touched her!" Mina complained, crossing her arms tightly.
Coach Rivera knelt down so their eyes were level.
"Maybe you did and maybe you didn't, but getting angry will not change the call," she said calmly.
"Right now, your anger is playing defense against you," she explained.
Then she taught Mina a simple trick: breathe in slowly, count to four, and breathe out.
Mina tried it three times, and her pounding heart gradually slowed down.
Eventually, she could hear her teammates cheering and see the scoreboard clearly.
Back on the court, she concentrated on the next play instead of the previous one.
With four seconds left, the Hawks trailed the Tigers by one point, 41 to 42.
Mina dribbled toward the basket, and a defender smacked her wrist.
This time the referee's whistle was on her side, so she earned two free throws.
Her first shot clanged off the rim, and the families in the stands groaned.
Mina felt the familiar anger bubbling up, but she breathed in, counted to four, and breathed out.
Her second shot swished through the net, tying the game and sending it to overtime.
The Hawks won by three points, and Mina announced that counting was her new secret weapon.

title: From a Car Trunk to a Waffle Sole
paragraphs: In 1964, a young runner named Phil Knight started a tiny shoe business with his old college track coach, Bill Bowerman.
Each man put in $500, and they called their new company Blue Ribbon Sports.
Knight had found a Japanese company called Onitsuka Tiger that made good running shoes at low prices.
He did not have a store yet, so he sold the shoes out of his car at high school track meets.
Bowerman coached runners at the University of Oregon.
He was always trying to make their shoes lighter and faster.
One morning in 1971, he stared at the bumpy grid on his family's waffle iron and came up with a wild idea.
He poured a rubbery liquid called urethane into the iron, hoping the little squares would make a sole that gripped the track.
The experiment ruined the waffle iron, which had been a wedding gift to his wife, Barbara.
Still, Bowerman kept testing, and his bumpy waffle pattern later became one of the most famous soles in running.
That same year, the company needed a logo for its very own brand of shoes.
Knight, who was teaching accounting at Portland State University, asked a design student named Carolyn Davidson for help.
She drew a curved shape that looks a bit like a checkmark.
People now call it the swoosh, and Davidson charged only $35 for it.
The new brand was named Nike, after the winged Greek goddess of victory.
Today, the swoosh is one of the best-known logos on the planet.
You can spot it on shoes, jerseys, and basketballs.
Nike grew from a car full of shoe boxes into one of the biggest sports companies in the world.
Its story shows that a giant business can start with a small idea, a little money, and even a kitchen tool.

title: Test, Fix, and Fly Again
paragraphs: Long before they built an airplane, Wilbur and Orville Wright ran a bicycle shop in Dayton, Ohio.
Fixing bikes taught them how light frames, chains, and gears work, and how a rider keeps a wobbly bike balanced.
The brothers wondered whether a flying machine could be balanced and steered in a similar way.
To find out, they spent hours carefully observing how birds glide, tilt, and turn high above the fields.
In 1900 and 1901, they tested gliders on the windy sand dunes of Kitty Hawk, North Carolina.
The gliders flew, but they did not lift nearly as well as the brothers had hoped.
Instead of giving up, the Wrights figured out that the numbers they had borrowed from another inventor did not fit their wings.
Back home, they built a wind tunnel, a wooden box with a fan that blew air over tiny model wings.
They tested more than 200 wing shapes and wrote down exactly how each one performed.
This slow, careful experimenting took weeks, but it finally gave them measurements they could trust.
With their new data, they designed a much better glider and, later, an airplane with its own engine.
On December 17, 1903, Orville lay on the lower wing at Kitty Hawk while Wilbur ran alongside the plane.
The machine rose into the strong wind and stayed in the air for about 12 seconds.
It traveled only 120 feet, which is shorter than the wings of a jumbo jet today.
The brothers took turns, and they made four flights that day.
Those short hops were the first times a powered airplane carried a pilot in a controlled flight.
The brothers did not succeed because they were lucky.
They succeeded because they tested their ideas, hunted down their mistakes, and fixed them again and again.
Their story proves that patience and careful experimenting can help people accomplish things that once seemed impossible.

title: The Gas That Keeps to Itself
paragraphs: Walk down a busy street at night, and you might see glowing signs that spell out words in bright red-orange light.
Many of these signs get their glow from neon, a gas that you cannot see, smell, or taste.
Neon belongs to a special family of elements called the noble gases.
Helium, neon, and argon are all members, and they sit together in group 18, the last column of the periodic table.
Noble gases are famous for keeping to themselves.
Most atoms are eager to grab, share, or give away electrons.
Electrons are the tiny particles that zoom around the outside of an atom.
The noble gases, however, already have a full outer shell of electrons, so they rarely react with other elements.
That is one reason helium fills party balloons instead of hydrogen, a gas that can catch fire.
To make a neon sign, workers heat glass tubes until they are soft and bend them into letters and shapes.
Next, they pump out the air and fill each tube with a small amount of neon gas.
When electricity passes through the tube, it gives the neon atoms extra energy.
The atoms quickly release that energy as red-orange light.
In 1910, a French inventor named Georges Claude showed off two glowing neon tubes, each 38 feet long, in Paris.
So how do some signs glow blue, green, or purple?
Pure argon gives off only a dim lavender light, so sign makers often add a tiny drop of mercury to it.
Clear tubes filled this way shine pale blue.
Tubes coated inside with powders called phosphors can glow in many other colors.
People call them all neon signs, but often only the red-orange ones are filled with pure neon.
The next time you see a glowing sign, see if you can guess which gas is hiding inside.

title: The Case of the Missing Basketball
paragraphs: On Monday morning, Mr. Lopez opened the equipment closet in Room 12 and frowned, because the class basketball was gone.
Without it, the big lunchtime game would have to be canceled.
Leo instantly decided that the fourth graders had taken it, since they had borrowed it once before.
His friend Mina did not want to jump to conclusions, so she asked if they could look for clues first.
Near the closet, Mina spotted a trail of dusty footprints with a zigzag pattern and a tiny star on each heel.
She pulled out her notebook and sketched the pattern so she would not forget a single detail.
The prints were small, much smaller than the sneakers worn by the fourth graders.
They led out the side door and toward the school garden, not toward the fourth-grade hallway.
Leo crouched down for a closer look and admitted that his guess was starting to look shaky.
Next, the two friends checked the gym timetable that was taped to the closet door.
It showed that the only class using the ball on Friday afternoon was a kindergarten class, from 2:00 to 2:30.
Below the timetable, someone had stuck a yellow note written in big, wobbly letters.
The note said that the ball had rolled into the muddy garden and that Room 3 was cleaning it before recess on Monday.
Mina remembered that Room 3 was the kindergarten class.
She also knew that sneakers with tiny stars were popular with the youngest students.
At recess, a group of kindergartners proudly carried the ball back, shiny and clean, and handed it to Mr. Lopez.
Leo grinned and confessed that his fast guess had been completely wrong.
Mina had cracked the case simply by reading every clue slowly and carefully.
From then on, whenever Leo felt like rushing, he reminded himself that a careful reader beats a fast guesser every time.
